blocks.text: Pagination lets an API return a large result set in manageable pages rather than all at once, relevant specifically to list-style LLM API endpoints, listing files, fine-tuning jobs, or stored assistant configurations, rather than the chat completion calls covered elsewhere in this module.

This topic covers cursor-based and offset-based pagination, page size limits, following a next page cursor correctly, fetching an entire result set across multiple pages, and why pagination matters for certain endpoints even though it rarely applies to a chat completion call itself.
1. What Pagination Solves

blocks.alt: Building on JSON payloads, pagination covers retrieving large lists in pages

blocks.text: Pagination exists because returning an enormous result set in a single response would be slow, memory intensive, and impractical, splitting a large list into smaller pages, retrieved one at a time, solves this cleanly.
2. Returning Everything at Once vs Paging Through Results

blocks.alt: Returning the full result set at once is compared against returning one page at a time

blocks.text: An endpoint listing every file you have ever uploaded, or every fine-tuning job you have ever run, could in principle return everything in one enormous response, in practice, providers instead return a manageable page of results at a time, with a mechanism to request the next page.
3. Cursor-Based vs Offset-Based Pagination

blocks.alt: Cursor based pagination uses a pointer to continue from, offset based uses a numeric position

blocks.text: Cursor-based pagination returns an opaque token pointing to exactly where to continue from on the next request, offset-based pagination instead uses a numeric position, skip the first fifty results, cursor-based is more common among modern LLM provider APIs since it handles data changing between requests more gracefully.

blocks.text: 4. Page Size Limits

blocks.alt: A requested page size gets bounded by the provider maximum limit

blocks.text: Most paginated endpoints let you request a specific page size, but cap it at some provider defined maximum, requesting a page size beyond that maximum typically either gets rejected or silently capped, worth checking the specific provider documentation for the actual limit.

code.content:
response = client.files.list(limit=100)  # capped at the provider maximum, whatever it is
next_cursor = response.get("next_cursor")

blocks.text: 5. Following the Next Page Cursor

blocks.alt: A first page response includes a next cursor, used for the next request

blocks.text: A paginated response typically includes a pointer to the next page, a cursor value or similar, alongside the actual page of results, your application passes that exact value into the next request to retrieve the following page, continuing until no further cursor is returned, signaling the last page has been reached.
6. Fetching an Entire Result Set

blocks.alt: A loop fetches each page until no more pages remain

blocks.text: A common pattern loops through pages automatically, requesting the next page using the previous response cursor, appending results to a running collection, and stopping once no further cursor is returned, giving your application the complete result set assembled from multiple individual page requests.

blocks.title: Many SDKs handle this looping automatically
blocks.content: This connects directly to SDKs, covered in an earlier module, many official provider SDKs expose an automatic pagination helper that iterates through every page transparently, sparing you from writing this loop by hand.

blocks.text: 7. Why Pagination Rarely Applies to Chat Completions

blocks.alt: The chat completion endpoint has no pagination, list endpoints are where pagination applies

blocks.text: A single chat completion call returns one response, not a list of many items, pagination genuinely applies to the list-style endpoints a provider offers, listing files, fine-tuning jobs, or stored configurations, not to the actual text generation calls that make up the bulk of most LLM API usage.
8. A Worked Pagination Example

An application needing to display every file a user has ever uploaded makes a first request for a page of results, receives a next cursor alongside that page, requests the next page using that cursor, and repeats until no further cursor is returned, assembling the complete file list across however many individual page requests that actually took.
9. Common Pagination Pitfalls

A common pitfall is assuming a first page alone represents the complete result set, silently missing later pages, another is manually reconstructing a cursor rather than passing the exact value the provider returned, which can produce unpredictable, unreliable pagination behavior.
Worked Example

A developer building a dashboard to display all fine-tuning jobs initially only requests the first page of results, the dashboard appears to work correctly during testing with a small number of jobs, but silently shows an incomplete list once a user accumulates enough jobs to span multiple pages.

Adding a proper pagination loop that follows the next cursor until no further pages remain fixes this silent data loss entirely, the dashboard now correctly displays every job regardless of how many pages the full result set actually spans.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming a single page response represents the complete result set without checking for a next page cursor
Manually reconstructing a pagination cursor instead of passing through the exact value the provider returned
Requesting a page size beyond the provider documented maximum and getting an unexpected result
Writing a custom pagination loop when an official SDK already provides an automatic pagination helper

blocks.text: Practice

Sketch out the loop logic for fetching an entire paginated result set, requesting a page, checking for a next cursor, and continuing until none remains, then consider how you would test this logic against a result set spanning exactly two pages.
Key Takeaway

Pagination lets a list-style endpoint return large result sets in manageable pages, typically using a cursor pointing to where the next page continues from, an application needs to follow this cursor through every page to retrieve a complete result set, and this concern applies specifically to list endpoints rather than the chat completion calls covered elsewhere in this module.
